records.notes: FR-040 boundary class for `exec`: a command that succeeds and writes NOTHING. Empty output is the edge of the stdout domain and is a different observation from output that was not captured — the distinction `present: false` exists to keep, and the one a comparison that treats empty as absent would silently lose.

SC-004 requires every operation to carry a case for each configuration source the applicability rules permit for it. `exec` against a Compose project has to reach the SERVICE container the configuration names, not the first container of the project. With a single service the two coincide, so the assertion is the round trip; the discrimination lives in the down cases, where a mis-identified project is observable.

Ports the `container-id` half of `parity_up_exec` and gives `bhv-exec-container-id-metadata` an INDEPENDENTLY REPORTED case — the thing its behavior record said was deferred (T110) because the declarative model had no way to name a container created mid-case. `${CONTAINER_ID}` is that way: the runner substitutes the id observed after `op-up`, and fails loud if an operation uses the token before any container exists, so the case cannot silently degrade into a workspace-addressed exec. The claim is #322: `exec --container-id` with NO `--workspace-folder` and NO `--config` has only the container to work from, so `remoteEnv` — which lives solely in devcontainer.json and is never baked into the image — is recoverable only if `up` stamped it into the `devcontainer.metadata` label and `exec` read it back. `FROM_CONTAINER_ENV` is asserted alongside it as the control: it reaches the process through the container's own environment either way, so a run where the metadata path is broken prints `remote=[] env=[baked-into-the-container]` rather than failing outright, and asserting only the exit code would call that a pass. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Migrated from parity_exec::tty: both CLIs present the same TTY allocation to the executed command. The same argv runs on both sides (the declarative model has one argv per operation), so the comparison is a true differential. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Migrated from parity_exec::user: both CLIs run the command as the same container user (an explicit `containerUser`). The same argv runs on both sides (the declarative model has one argv per operation), so the comparison is a true differential. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Migrated from parity_exec::working-directory: both CLIs run the command in the same container working directory (an explicit `workspaceFolder`). The same argv runs on both sides (the declarative model has one argv per operation), so the comparison is a true differential. Image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-exec-dockerfile-running-cli-overlay`. Three sources of environment meet in one invocation — the image's own `ENV`, the configuration's `containerEnv`, and a `--remote-env` overlay — and all three must survive together. The `command -v conf-tool` PATH probe that used to share this argv now lives in case-exec-image-path-overlay. Splitting them was forced by the tolerance model, not by preference: the probe DOES diverge (deacon loses the image's `ENV PATH`), the divergence lands in arbitrary stdout TEXT, and a tolerance over the whole of `chan-stdout` is a wildcard by any reading — which is exactly why `chan-stdout` is excluded from SCALAR_OBSERVABLE. Keeping both subjects in one case would have meant either weakening that rule or letting a real divergence sit uncharacterized. Each case now has one subject, and the exit-code tolerance in the sibling is scoped to a case whose only exit code IS the PATH probe.

Pins what deacon's PATH restoration (#370) produces when BOTH an image `ENV PATH=` entry and a Feature's `/etc/profile.d` entry are in play — the case the fix's design question turned on. Deliberately spec-expectation, not live-differential: the reference produces `/opt/feature/bin:/opt/image/bin:…` for this input, so a differential would fail on `chan-stdout`, and `chan-stdout` is un-waivable by design (its diverging path is the bare channel id, and a whole-channel tolerance is a wildcard). Asserting deacon's own output states what deacon does without claiming a cross-CLI agreement that does not hold. Both tools are then RUN, not just listed: an ordering assertion alone would still pass if a directory were on PATH but unreachable, and `image-tool`/`feature-tool` exiting 0 is what proves each contributor actually resolves. The measured reference ordering lives in `bhv-exec-restored-path-ordering`; image pinned to alpine:3.19 (V18).

The PATH half of the exec/dockerfile/cli-overlay pair, split out of case-exec-dockerfile-overlay so the divergence it carries is addressable by a scoped tolerance. The argv resolves the tool THROUGH A SHELL (`sh -c conf-tool`) rather than naming it as the exec argv, because those are two different lookups and only one of them is broken: `docker exec` resolves a bare argv against the container's own configuration and finds the tool on both sides, so `-- conf-tool` would pass vacuously. A shell inside the session reads `$PATH` as deacon handed it over, which is where the image's entry has gone missing — deacon exits 127, the reference runs the tool and exits 0. `sh -c` rather than `sh -lc` for the same reason: a login shell re-sources `/etc/profile`, which would put a third PATH in play and blur what the case is measuring. The earlier `command -v conf-tool` form was worse still — `command` is a shell BUILTIN, so as an exec argv it is not an executable at all and both CLIs failed identically with 127, agreeing about nothing. Characterized by bhv-exec-image-path-preserved / wvr-exec-image-path-dropped, tracked for fix at https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/370. No `scenarioContext`: the triple this exercises is already carried by its sibling, and declaring it twice would inflate the pairwise denominator with a combination nothing new is being learned about. When the fix lands, the tolerance stops being consumed and is reported stale, which is what forces it to be deleted alongside.

FR-040 malformed class for `exec`: the target container is identified from the configuration, so a document that cannot be parsed stops the run before any container is looked up. The container-state is `none` deliberately — the case never gets far enough for one to exist.

allowedDifferences.rationale: deacon rejects the document before a container exists, so the exec never runs; the reference execs successfully in the container it created.

records.notes: FR-040 reference-lenient class for `exec`: the reference accepts a wrongly-typed `forwardPorts`, creates the container and then execs into it successfully; deacon refuses the document and never reaches the container. Same fixture, same waiver, one stage further along than the `up` case — which is the evidence that the leniency is not a read-time quirk.

Ports `parity_exec::env-propagation` (res-exec-per-side-argv). A variable supplied with `--remote-env` must reach the command's environment on both sides. The residual recorded a need for PER-SIDE argument vectors, which was disproven: deacon declares `--remote-env` as the primary flag with `--env` as a legacy alias, so ONE shared argv exercises both CLIs. Measured before this case was written — both print `BAR`. Asserting stdout (not just the exit code) is the point: an exec that dropped the variable would still exit 0 and print an empty line.

FR-040 unsupported class for `exec`: the invocation is well-formed and the container is running, but the named executable does not exist inside it. Both CLIs must surface the container's own failure rather than substitute one of their own, and the exit code is where that shows.

`exec` is a transport: the command's exit code is the CLI's exit code, unchanged. 123 is chosen for being unmistakably the COMMAND's — not 0, not 1, and not 127, which a missing binary produces on its own and which `case-exec-unsupported-missing-command` already covers. The distinction that matters is 'forwards the exact code' versus 'reports failure as 1', and only a specific, arbitrary code can tell them apart.

Mined from the reference's own e2e suite (`src/test/cli.exec.base.ts` at v0.87.0, 'should return exit code without terminal'), where it is pinned twice — once piped and once under a PTY. Measured on this sequence at oracle 0.87.0 before the case was written: both CLIs exit 123.

DELIBERATELY `spec-expectation` rather than `live-differential`, which is where 11 of the 13 pre-existing `exec` cases sit. The precedent is #570's: the differential lane runs nightly and GATES NOTHING, so a behavior worth protecting from regression belongs in a lane that gates every pull request. The reference measurement is what established the expectation; pinning deacon's own side is what enforces it. Nothing is lost by not re-running the reference here — the oracle is pinned at 0.87.0, so its answer cannot drift underneath us without a deliberate bump.

argv: printf 'set=[%s]\n' "$PARITY_SET"; if [ -n "${PARITY_EMPTY+present}" ]; then printf 'empty=present:[%s]\n' "$PARITY_EMPTY"; else echo 'empty=ABSENT'; fi

records.notes:
`--remote-env NAME=` sets NAME to the EMPTY STRING; it does not decline to set it. The two outcomes are invisible to `printf "$NAME"` — both print nothing — so the probe uses `${NAME+present}`, which expands only when the variable EXISTS. Getting this wrong in either direction is a silent behavior change for anything that tests a variable's presence rather than its value, which is ordinary shell practice.

Mined from `src/test/cli.exec.base.ts` at v0.87.0 ('should pass along --remote-env'), which pins `--remote-env FOO=BAR --remote-env BAZ=` and asserts `env.BAZ === ''` — an assertion that only holds if the key is present with an empty value. `case-exec-remote-env-propagation` already covers the ordinary `FOO=BAR` half; the empty-value tail is what was missing, and it is the half with an edge in it.

Both flags are passed in one invocation on purpose: a parser that mishandles the empty value could also swallow the pair that follows it, and asserting both in one line catches that. Measured at oracle 0.87.0: both CLIs report `set=[value]` and `empty=present:[]`. `spec-expectation` for the reason given in `case-exec-exit-code-passthrough`.

With no `--workspace-folder`, `exec` targets the container for the CURRENT DIRECTORY. This is the shape a developer actually types — `cd` into the project and run `deacon exec …` — and every other `exec` case passes the flag explicitly, so nothing covered it.

It costs nothing to express: the runner already invokes each operation with its cwd set to the case's isolated workspace (`runner.rs`, `run_and_capture(… &workspace …)`), so OMITTING the flag is the whole test. That is also the case's one fragility, recorded here because it is not visible in the argv: if the runner ever stops anchoring cwd to the workspace, this case starts failing for a reason that has nothing to do with `exec`.

Mined from `src/test/cli.exec.base.ts` at v0.87.0, which covers it twice — 'should exec with default workspace folder (current directory)' and the negative 'should fail gracefully when no config in current directory and no container-id'. Measured at oracle 0.87.0: both CLIs succeed. `spec-expectation` for the reason given in `case-exec-exit-code-passthrough`.

`exec --config` selects WHICH document in the workspace to act on, and its `remoteEnv` is what the executed command sees. The fixture's two documents differ only in that one value — root says `root`, subfolder says `subfolder` — so the assertion cannot pass by accident: reading the discovered document instead of the named one produces `config=[root]`, and reading neither produces `config=[]`. A fixture with only the subfolder document would have passed all three ways.

Mined from `src/test/cli.exec.base.ts` at v0.87.0 ('should exec with config in subfolder'), which does exactly this — `up --config …/subfolder/devcontainer.json` then `exec --config …` reading a `remoteEnv` the subfolder document alone declares.

This is the shape that surfaced [#584](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/584): putting two documents in one workspace is what exposed the supersede sweep stopping siblings. This case does NOT assert that — `case-up-sibling-config-both-running` does, on the container census where it belongs. Here the second document exists only so that naming one is a real choice. Measured at oracle 0.87.0: both CLIs print `config=[subfolder]`.

A `--workspace-folder` that does not exist fails with exit 1 rather than a panic, a zero exit, or a shell-level code. `case-exec-malformed-config-rejected` covers a config that exists and is unparseable; this covers the path not being there at all, which reaches a different code path (workspace resolution, before any config load).

Mined from `src/test/cli.exec.base.ts` at v0.87.0, which asserts `error.code === 1` and a `Dev container config (…) not found.` message.

HERMETIC, not `docker-shared` — the only `exec` case that is. The failure happens during workspace resolution, BEFORE any config load and before any daemon contact, so the case needs nothing and belongs in the lane that runs on every profile including `dev-fast` and on all three operating systems, rather than in one that waits for a daemon. Precedent is `case-errors-decl-bad-config-path-decision`, which is the same shape for `read-configuration`. Verified under `unshare -rn` with the rest of `parity_hermetic`.

Both channels pin DEACON's answer rather than compare it, which is what `spec-expectation` means and is why the diagnostic can be asserted here at all: the two CLIs word this differently — deacon says `Failed to resolve workspace path '<abs>': path does not exist or cannot be accessed`, the reference `Dev container config (<abs>/.devcontainer/devcontainer.json) not found.` Both name the problem and both exit 1, and deacon's names the directory it could not resolve rather than a file it never looked for, which is the more accurate of the two. So the wording difference is not a divergence to fix, and pinning deacon's own phrasing costs nothing while stopping the diagnostic from quietly evaporating into a bare exit code. A `live-differential` here would need a tolerance to say only that the two disagree about wording, which is worth less than what this asserts.
